claim: After exocytosis, release sites are cleared of vesicular residues to replenish with transmitter-filled vesicles.
source: After exocytosis, release sites are cleared of vesicular residues to replenish with transmitter-filled vesicles.
evidence: This is a general statement about synaptic mechanisms that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Endocytic and scaffold proteins are thought to underlie the site-clearance mechanism.
source: Endocytic and scaffold proteins are thought to underlie this site-clearance mechanism.
evidence: This statement reflects current scientific understanding and speculation about the molecular mechanisms involved.

claim: Pharmacological block of endocytosis enhanced synaptic depression at the calyx synapse.
source: Pharmacological block of endocytosis enhanced synaptic depression at the calyx synapse, whereas it attenuated synaptic facilitation at the hippocampal synapse.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing effects of endocytic blockers on synaptic responses.

claim: Pharmacological block of endocytosis attenuated synaptic facilitation at the hippocampal synapse.
source: Pharmacological block of endocytosis enhanced synaptic depression at the calyx synapse, whereas it attenuated synaptic facilitation at the hippocampal synapse.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing effects of endocytic blockers on hippocampal synaptic responses.

claim: Block of scaffold protein activity enhanced synaptic depression at the calyx synapse.
source: Block of scaffold protein activity likewise enhanced synaptic depression at the calyx but had no effect at the hippocampal synapse.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of scaffold protein inhibitors on calyceal synaptic responses.

claim: Block of scaffold protein activity had no effect at the hippocampal synapse.
source: Block of scaffold protein activity likewise enhanced synaptic depression at the calyx but had no effect at the hippocampal synapse.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing lack of effect of scaffold protein inhibitors on hippocampal synaptic responses.

claim: At the fast calyx synapse, block of endocytosis or scaffold protein activity significantly enhanced synaptic depression as early as 10 ms after the stimulation onset.
source: At the fast calyx synapse, block of endocytosis or scaffold protein activity significantly enhanced synaptic depression as early as 10 ms after the stimulation onset.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing rapid effects of blockers on synaptic depression.

claim: Neither endocytic blockers nor scaffold protein inhibitors prolonged the recovery from short-term depression.
source: Unlike previous reports, neither endocytic blockers nor scaffold protein inhibitors prolonged the recovery from short-term depression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on recovery kinetics and contrasts with previous findings.

claim: The release-site clearance by endocytosis can be a universal phenomenon supporting vesicle replenishment at both fast and slow synapses.
source: We conclude that the release-site clearance by endocytosis can be a universal phenomenon supporting vesicle replenishment at both fast and slow synapses, whereas the presynaptic scaffold mechanism likely plays a specialized role in vesicle replenishment predominantly at fast synapses.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing endocytic effects at both calyx and hippocampal synapses.

claim: The presynaptic scaffold mechanism likely plays a specialized role in vesicle replenishment predominantly at fast synapses.
source: We conclude that the release-site clearance by endocytosis can be a universal phenomenon supporting vesicle replenishment at both fast and slow synapses, whereas the presynaptic scaffold mechanism likely plays a specialized role in vesicle replenishment predominantly at fast synapses.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing differential effects of scaffold inhibitors at fast versus slow synapses.

claim: Following inactivation of the temperature-sensitive endocytic protein dynamin in Drosophila mutant Shibire, short-term depression (STD) of neuromuscular synaptic currents evoked by action potentials (APs) are enhanced within 20 ms from the stimulation onset at 33°C.
source: Following inactivation of the temperature-sensitive endocytic protein dynamin in Drosophila mutant Shibire, short-term depression (STD) of neuromuscular synaptic currents evoked by action potentials (APs) are enhanced within 20 ms from the stimulation onset at 33°C (Kawasaki et al., 2000), suggesting that endocytosis plays a significant role in rapid release site-clearance in addition to its well-established role in vesicle recycling (Neher and Sakaba, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Kawasaki et al., 2000.

claim: Endocytosis plays a significant role in rapid release site-clearance in addition to its well-established role in vesicle recycling.
source: Following inactivation of the temperature-sensitive endocytic protein dynamin in Drosophila mutant Shibire, short-term depression (STD) of neuromuscular synaptic currents evoked by action potentials (APs) are enhanced within 20 ms from the stimulation onset at 33°C (Kawasaki et al., 2000), suggesting that endocytosis plays a significant role in rapid release site-clearance in addition to its well-established role in vesicle recycling (Neher and Sakaba, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kawasaki et al., 2000 and Neher and Sakaba, 2008, and represents an inference from the cited work.

claim: The enhancement of STD by blocking endocytosis was reproduced at the calyx of Held in slices from rodent brainstem, associated with a pronounced prolongation in the recovery from STD of EPSCs evoked by paired command pulses under voltage clamp.
source: The enhancement of STD by blocking endocytosis was reproduced at the calyx of Held in slices from rodent brainstem, associated with a pronounced prolongation in the recovery from STD of EPSCs evoked by paired command pulses under voltage clamp (Hosoi et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Hosoi et al., 2009.

claim: Fluorescence imaging with synaptopHluorin at cultured hippocampal synapses showed that endocytic blockers, but not the vesicle acidification blockers, enhance steady state depression of exocytosis induced by high-frequency stimulation.
source: Fluorescence imaging with synaptopHluorin at cultured hippocampal synapses also showed that endocytic blockers, but not the vesicle acidification blockers, enhance steady state depression of exocytosis induced by high-frequency stimulation, suggesting slow clearance of vesicular component from release-sites (Hua et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Hua et al., 2013.

claim: Genetic ablation of the endocytic adaptor protein AP-2μ enhances STD.
source: Also, in cell culture studies, genetic ablation of the endocytic adaptor protein AP-2μ (Jung et al., 2015), synaptophysin (Rajappa et al., 2016), or the secretory carrier membrane protein SCAMP5 (Park et al., 2018) enhances STD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jung et al., 2015.

claim: Genetic ablation of synaptophysin enhances STD.
source: Also, in cell culture studies, genetic ablation of the endocytic adaptor protein AP-2μ (Jung et al., 2015), synaptophysin (Rajappa et al., 2016), or the secretory carrier membrane protein SCAMP5 (Park et al., 2018) enhances STD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rajappa et al., 2016.

claim: Genetic ablation of the secretory carrier membrane protein SCAMP5 enhances STD.
source: Also, in cell culture studies, genetic ablation of the endocytic adaptor protein AP-2μ (Jung et al., 2015), synaptophysin (Rajappa et al., 2016), or the secretory carrier membrane protein SCAMP5 (Park et al., 2018) enhances STD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Park et al., 2018.

claim: The presynaptic scaffold protein intersectin is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, which activates the Rho-GTPase CDC42, thereby regulating the filamentous (F) actin assembly.
source: The presynaptic scaffold protein intersectin is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, which activates the Rho-GTPase CDC42, thereby regulating the filamentous (F) actin assembly (Hussain et al., 2001; Marie et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hussain et al., 2001 and Marie et al., 2004.

claim: At the calyx of Held in slices from pre-hearing rodents, genetic ablation of intersectin 1 or pharmacological block of CDC42 abolishes the fast component of the rate of recovery from STD of EPSCs evoked by a pair of square pulses.
source: At the calyx of Held in slices from pre-hearing rodents, genetic ablation of intersectin 1 or pharmacological block of CDC42 abolishes the fast component of the rate of recovery from STD of EPSCs evoked by a pair of square pulses (Sakaba et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sakaba et al., 2013.

claim: The scaffold protein cascade, comprising intersectin, CDC42, and F-actin, contributes to rapid vesicle replenishment, possibly through release site-clearance.
source: They suggest that the scaffold protein cascade, comprising intersectin, CDC42, and F-actin, contributes to rapid vesicle replenishment, possibly through release site-clearance (Jäpel et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jäpel et al., 2020 and represents an inference from that work.

claim: The post-hearing calyx of Held is a fast-signaling auditory relay synapse that can respond to inputs up to 500 Hz without failure in vivo.
source: The post-hearing calyx of Held is a fast-signaling auditory relay synapse that can respond to inputs up to 500 Hz without failure in vivo (Sonntag et al., 2009) and displays STD during repetitive stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sonntag et al., 2009.

claim: The post-hearing calyx of Held displays STD during repetitive stimulation.
source: The post-hearing calyx of Held is a fast-signaling auditory relay synapse that can respond to inputs up to 500 Hz without failure in vivo (Sonntag et al., 2009) and displays STD during repetitive stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about the calyx of Held synapse.

claim: The hippocampal synapse from Schaffer collaterals (SCs) to pyramidal cells (PCs) in the CA1 area is a relatively slow synapse that starts to fail transmission already at 40 Hz in slice.
source: In contrast, the hippocampal synapse from Schaffer collaterals (SCs) to pyramidal cells (PCs) in the CA1 area is a relatively slow synapse that starts to fail transmission already at 40 Hz in slice (Combe et al., 2018) and at 37°C and in 1.3 mM [Ca2+], short-term facilitation masks depression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Combe et al., 2018.

claim: At the hippocampal CA1 synapse at 37°C and in 1.3 mM [Ca2+], short-term facilitation masks depression.
source: In contrast, the hippocampal synapse from Schaffer collaterals (SCs) to pyramidal cells (PCs) in the CA1 area is a relatively slow synapse that starts to fail transmission already at 40 Hz in slice (Combe et al., 2018) and at 37°C and in 1.3 mM [Ca2+], short-term facilitation masks depression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Dynasore is a dynamin-dependent endocytosis blocker blocking both clathrin-mediated and clathrin-independent endocytosis.
source: Dynasore is a dynamin-dependent endocytosis blocker (Macia et al., 2006; Newton et al., 2006) blocking both clathrin-mediated and clathrin-independent endocytosis (Park et al., 2013; Delvendahl et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Pitstop-2 is thought to preferentially block clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: A second endocytosis blocker Pitstop-2 is thought to preferentially block clathrin-mediated endocytosis (von Kleist et al., 2011; Delvendahl et al., 2016; López-Hernández et al., 2022) but it reportedly blocks clathrin-independent endocytosis as well (Dutta et al., 2012; Willox et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pitstop-2 reportedly blocks clathrin-independent endocytosis as well.
source: A second endocytosis blocker Pitstop-2 is thought to preferentially block clathrin-mediated endocytosis (von Kleist et al., 2011; Delvendahl et al., 2016; López-Hernández et al., 2022) but it reportedly blocks clathrin-independent endocytosis as well (Dutta et al., 2012; Willox et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dutta et al., 2012 and Willox et al., 2014.

claim: At calyces of Held, a single short (5 ms) command pulse elicited an exocytic capacitance jump (ΔCm) followed by a slow endocytosis (29 fF/s in decay rate).
source: At calyces of Held, a single short (5 ms) command pulse elicited an exocytic capacitance jump (ΔCm) followed by a slow endocytosis (29 fF/s in decay rate, Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the presence of Dynasore (100 μM) or Pitstop-2 (25 μM), slow endocytic membrane recovery was almost completely blocked, whereas ΔCm or presynaptic Ca2+ current was unchanged.
source: In the presence of Dynasore (100 μM) or Pitstop-2 (25 μM) in the perfusate (within 10–60 min of application), this slow endocytic membrane recovery was almost completely blocked, whereas ΔCm or presynaptic Ca2+ current was unchanged (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Dynasore or Pitstop-2 significantly inhibited the maximal rate of 250 fF/s of accelerated fast endocytosis (20 ms x 15 times at 1 Hz) to ~50%.
source: Dynasore or Pitstop-2 significantly inhibited the maximal rate of 250 fF/s of this accelerated fast endocytosis (20 ms x 15 times at 1 Hz) to ~50% (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 10 command pulses (20 ms duration) applied at 10 Hz induced a fast endocytosis with a decay rate (350 fF/s) by more than 10 times faster than the slow endocytosis elicited by a 5 ms pulse.
source: In another stimulation protocol (Figure 1C), 10 command pulses (20 ms duration) applied at 10 Hz induced a fast endocytosis with a decay rate (350 fF/s) by more than 10 times faster than the slow endocytosis elicited by a 5 ms pulse (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A and 1C.

claim: Dynasore or Pitstop-2 significantly inhibited the rate of fast endocytosis induced by 10 Hz stimulation.
source: Dynasore or Pitstop-2 significantly inhibited the rate of this fast endocytosis (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1) too.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The potencies of bath-applied Dynasore or Pitstop-2 for blocking slow and fast forms of endocytosis were comparable to that of dynamin-1 proline-rich domain peptide (Dyn-1 PRD peptide) directly loaded in calyceal terminals (1 mM).
source: The potencies of bath-applied Dynasore or Pitstop-2 for blocking slow and fast forms of endocytosis were comparable to that of dynamin-1 proline-rich domain peptide (Dyn-1 PRD peptide) directly loaded in calyceal terminals (1 mM; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Yamashita et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Yamashita et al., 2005.

claim: At the calyx of Held, bath-application of Dynasore or Pitstop-2 can block both fast and slow endocytosis to a similar extent as direct presynaptic whole-cell loading of Dyn-1 PRD peptide without perturbing presynaptic intracellular milieu.
source: Thus, at calyces of Held, bath-application of Dynasore or Pitstop-2 can block both fast and slow endocytosis to a similar extent as direct presynaptic whole-cell loading of Dyn-1 PRD peptide without perturbing presynaptic intracellular milieu.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data comparing bath-applied drugs to intracellular peptide loading.

claim: Neither Dynasore nor Pitstop-2 affected the first EPSC amplitude in the train at the calyx of Held.
source: Neither Dynasore nor Pitstop-2 (in the perfusate, within 10–60 min of application) affected the first EPSC amplitude in the train (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: During a train of stimulations at 10 Hz, in the presence of Dynasore (100 μM), synaptic depression was marginally enhanced (from 45% to 52%, with no significant difference), but Pitstop-2 had no effect.
source: During a train of stimulations at 10 Hz, in the presence of Dynasore (100 μM), synaptic depression was marginally enhanced (from 45% to 52%, with no significant difference), but Pitstop-2 had no effect (Figure 2A1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A1.

claim: At 100 Hz stimulations, both Dynasore and Pitstop-2 markedly and equally enhanced synaptic depression starting at 10 ms (2nd stimulation) from the stimulus onset, increasing the magnitude of steady state STD (averaged from #26–30 EPSCs) from 58% to 75% (1.3 times; p<0.001, t-test).
source: At 100 Hz stimulations, however, both Dynasore and Pitstop-2 markedly and equally enhanced synaptic depression starting at 10 ms (2nd stimulation) from the stimulus onset, increasing the magnitude of steady state STD (averaged from #26–30 EPSCs) from 58% to 75% (1.3 times; p<0.001, t-test; Figure 2B1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B1.

claim: Endocytosis-dependent rapid SV replenishment operates during high-frequency transmission at the mammalian central synapses like at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of Drosophila.
source: These results suggest that endocytosis-dependent rapid SV replenishment operates during high-frequency transmission at the mammalian central synapses like at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of Drosophila (Kawasaki et al., 2000).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data and compared to previous findings in Drosophila.

claim: Glutamate released during action potential evoked EPSCs does not desensitize or saturate postsynaptic receptors at post-hearing calyces of Held.
source: Since glutamate released during action potential evoked EPSCs does not desensitize or saturate postsynaptic receptors at post-hearing calyces of Held (Ishikawa et al., 2002) unlike at pre-hearing calyces (Yamashita et al., 2009), enhanced synaptic depression in the presence of endocytic blockers during repetitive fiber stimulations is most likely caused by presynaptic mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ishikawa et al., 2002.

claim: Enhanced synaptic depression in the presence of endocytic blockers during repetitive fiber stimulations is most likely caused by presynaptic mechanisms.
source: Since glutamate released during action potential evoked EPSCs does not desensitize or saturate postsynaptic receptors at post-hearing calyces of Held (Ishikawa et al., 2002) unlike at pre-hearing calyces (Yamashita et al., 2009), enhanced synaptic depression in the presence of endocytic blockers during repetitive fiber stimulations is most likely caused by presynaptic mechanisms.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data and the cited literature about receptor properties.

claim: The results of the endocytic block were essentially the same in the absence or presence of the low-affinity glutamate receptor ligand kynurenic acid (1 mM).
source: In fact, the results of the endocytic block were essentially the same in the absence (Figure 2) or presence (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) of the low-affinity glutamate receptor ligand kynurenic acid (1 mM), which reduces postsynaptic receptor occupancy with glutamate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: At post-hearing calyces in 1.3 mM [Ca2+] and at PT (37°C), the endocytic blockers did not prolong the recovery of AP evoked EPSCs from STD.
source: In contrast, at post-hearing calyces in 1.3 mM [Ca2+] and at PT (37°C), the endocytic blockers did not prolong the recovery of AP evoked EPSCs from STD (Figure 2A2 and B2, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A2 and 2B2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The recovery from STD caused by 100 Hz stimulation was significantly accelerated at both fast and slow recovery components in the presence of endocytic blockers.
source: Conversely, the recovery from STD caused by 100 Hz stimulation was significantly accelerated at both fast and slow recovery components (Figure 2B2, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Genetic ablation of intersectin inhibits endocytosis in cultured synapses.
source: Genetic ablation of intersectin inhibits endocytosis in cultured synapses (Yu et al., 2008), but does not affect endocytosis at pre-hearing calyces of Held (Sakaba et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2008.

claim: Genetic ablation of intersectin does not affect endocytosis at pre-hearing calyces of Held.
source: Genetic ablation of intersectin inhibits endocytosis in cultured synapses (Yu et al., 2008), but does not affect endocytosis at pre-hearing calyces of Held (Sakaba et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sakaba et al., 2013.

claim: ML141 or Latrunculin-B had no effect on slow endocytosis, fast accelerating endocytosis, or fast endocytosis at the post-hearing calyx of Held.
source: In agreement with previous report (Sakaba et al., 2013), none of these inhibitors affected the fast or slow forms of endocytosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and citation to Sakaba et al., 2013.

claim: Neither ML141 nor Latrunculin-B affected the first EPSC amplitude in the train at the calyx of Held.
source: We then recorded EPSCs in 1.3 mM [Ca2+] at PT. Neither ML141 nor Latrunculin-B affected the first EPSC amplitude in the train (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), alike Latrunculin-B effects at RT and 2.0 mM [Ca2+] (Mahapatra et al., 2016; Mahapatra and Lou, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and citations to previous work.

claim: During a train of stimulations at 10 Hz or 100 Hz, in the presence of ML141 or Latrunculin-B in perfusates, synaptic depression was markedly and equally enhanced.
source: During a train of stimulations at 10 Hz (Figure 4A1) or 100 Hz (Figure 4B1), in the presence of ML141 or Latrunculin-B in perfusates, synaptic depression was markedly and equally enhanced, with STD magnitude (#26–30) increasing from 45% to 62% (1.4 times; P<0.001, t-test; Figure 4A1) at 10 Hz and from 58% to 80% at 100 Hz (1.4 times; p<0.001, t-test; Figure 4B1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A1 and 4B1.

claim: In contrast to endocytic blockers, the STD-enhancing effect of scaffold protein inhibitors was stronger and independent of stimulation frequency.
source: In contrast to the endocytic blockers (Figure 2), the STD-enhancing effect of scaffold protein inhibitors was stronger and independent of stimulation frequency (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Co-application of endocytic and scaffold protein cascade inhibitors revealed that the synaptic strengthening effects of endocytosis and scaffold machinery are complementary rather than additive.
source: Co-application of endocytic and scaffold protein cascade inhibitors revealed that the synaptic strengthening effects of endocytosis and scaffold machinery are complementary rather than additive (Figure 5C).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Fast endocytosis quickly clears vesicle residues, whereas scaffold machinery simultaneously mobilizes and replenishes transmitter-filled vesicles to release sites during high-frequency transmission.
source: These results together suggest that fast endocytosis quickly clears vesicle residues, whereas scaffold machinery simultaneously mobilizes and replenishes transmitter-filled vesicles to release sites during high-frequency transmission (Figure 7).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Through combinatory mechanisms of endocytosis and scaffold machinery, synaptic strength and high-fidelity neurotransmission (up to 500 Hz) can be maintained at fast synapses such as the calyx of Held auditory relay synapse.
source: Through these combinatory mechanisms, synaptic strength and high-fidelity neurotransmission (up to 500 Hz; Sonntag et al., 2009) can be maintained at fast synapses such as the calyx of Held auditory relay synapse.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data and cited literature about high-frequency transmission.

claim: Under physiological conditions in slices, short-term plasticity at hippocampal CA1 synapses was facilitatory, in contrast to depression at calyceal synapses.
source: Under physiological conditions in slices, short-term plasticity at hippocampal CA1 synapses was facilitatory, in contrast to depression at calyceal synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Endocytic blockers attenuated the synaptic facilitation at hippocampal CA1 synapses, suggesting that endocytosis boosts synaptic facilitation at this synapse.
source: Endocytic blockers attenuated the synaptic facilitation, suggesting that endocytosis boosts synaptic facilitation at this synapse (Figure 6).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Dynasore significantly enhanced the basal EPSC amplitude at hippocampal CA1 synapses.
source: Unexpectedly, Dynasore significantly enhanced the basal EPSC amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), whereas Pitstop-2 had no such effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pitstop-2 had no effect on basal EPSC amplitude at hippocampal CA1 synapses.
source: Unexpectedly, Dynasore significantly enhanced the basal EPSC amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), whereas Pitstop-2 had no such effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pitstop-2 significantly attenuated synaptic facilitation at hippocampal CA1 synapses, although less potent than Dynasore.
source: Although less potent than Dynasore, Pitstop-2 significantly attenuated synaptic facilitation (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: At hippocampal CA1 synapses, the scaffold protein inhibitor ML141 or Latrunculin B had no effect on EPSC facilitation.
source: In clear contrast to fast calyceal synapses, the scaffold protein inhibitor ML141 or Latrunculin B had no effect on EPSC facilitation at relatively slow hippocampal CA1 synapses (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: Physiologically, the vesicle acidification mechanism is not involved in the short-term synaptic efficacy at hippocampal CA1 synapses.
source: Thus, physiologically, the vesicle acidification mechanism is not involved in the short-term synaptic efficacy at hippocampal CA1 synapses.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing no effect of vesicle acidification blockers.

claim: At the calyx of Held in slices under physiologically optimized conditions, blocking endocytosis by bath-application of Dynasore or Pitstop-2 enhanced activity dependent short-term depression of EPSCs evoked by high-frequency afferent fiber stimulations.
source: At the calyx of Held in slices under physiologically optimized conditions, blocking endocytosis by bath-application of Dynasore or Pitstop-2 enhanced activity dependent short-term depression of EPSCs evoked by high-frequency afferent fiber stimulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The enhancement of synaptic depression by endocytic blockers was significant already at the 2nd EPSC (10 ms) after the stimulation onset and proceeded bi-exponentially with a fast (5–6 ms) and slow (24–35 ms) time constant.
source: This enhancement of synaptic depression was significant already at the 2nd EPSC (10 ms) after the stimulation onset and proceeded bi-exponentially with a fast (5–6 ms) and slow (24–35 ms) time constant (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The slow time constants of synaptic depression in the presence of endocytic blockers were comparable to control time constant (37 ms) undergoing mono-exponential depression.
source: These slow time constants were comparable to control time constant (37 ms) undergoing mono-exponential depression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: The depression-counteracting effect of endocytosis was restricted to the early epoch of high-frequency transmission when many vesicle residues occupy the release sites.
source: Thus, the depression-counteracting effect of endocytosis was restricted to the early epoch of high-frequency transmission when many vesicle residues occupy the release sites.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing time-dependent effects.

claim: At the calyx of Held, Dynasore or Pitstop-2 blocked both fast and slow endocytosis.
source: At the calyx of Held, Dynasore or Pitstop-2 blocked both fast and slow endocytosis (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The fast endocytosis is characterized with a rate of ~350 fF/s, which was slowed by endocytic blockers to ~150 fF/s.
source: The fast endocytosis is characterized with a rate of ~350 fF/s, which was slowed by endocytic blockers to ~150 fF/s (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The reduction of endocytic rate (200 fF/s) corresponds to 2.54 vesicles/ms (1 fF = 12.7 vesicles).
source: This reduction of endocytic rate (200 fF/s) corresponds to 2.54 vesicles/ms (1 fF = 12.7 vesicles; Yamashita et al., 2010; 200 fF/s x 12.7 vesicles x 1/1000ms).
evidence: This calculation is based on experimental data and citation to Yamashita et al., 2010 for the conversion factor.

claim: The mean amplitude of miniature EPSCs, representing a single vesicle response, was ~55 pA in 1.3 mM [Ca2+] at PT.
source: Since the mean amplitude of miniature EPSCs, representing a single vesicle response, was ~55 pA in 1.3 mM [Ca 2+] at PT (data not shown), endocytic block is estimated to reduce EPSC amplitude by ~1.4 nA in 10 ms (2.54 vesicles/ms x 55 pA x 10 ms x 1/1000 nA).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data that was not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Endocytic block is estimated to reduce EPSC amplitude by ~1.4 nA in 10 ms.
source: Since the mean amplitude of miniature EPSCs, representing a single vesicle response, was ~55 pA in 1.3 mM [Ca 2+] at PT (data not shown), endocytic block is estimated to reduce EPSC amplitude by ~1.4 nA in 10 ms (2.54 vesicles/ms x 55 pA x 10 ms x 1/1000 nA).
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data and represents an inference.

claim: The estimated reduction in EPSC amplitude by endocytic block (~1.4 nA) is close to the average amplitude difference between control and endocytic blockers (1.6 nA) at the 2nd EPSC (10 ms after the 1st EPSC) under 100 Hz stimulation.
source: This is close to the average amplitude difference between control and endocytic blockers (1.6 nA) at the 2nd EPSC (10 ms after the 1st EPSC) under 100 Hz stimulation (Figure 2B1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This comparison is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: During high-frequency transmission, the site-clearance by fast endocytosis can fully compensate the initial strong depression.
source: Therefore, during high-frequency transmission, the site-clearance by fast endocytosis can fully compensate the initial strong depression.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the quantitative analysis of experimental data.

claim: The rate of slow endocytosis (29 fF/s) is ~10 times slower than fast endocytosis (250–350 fF/s).
source: However, the rate of slow endocytosis (29 fF/s) is ~10 times slower than fast endocytosis (250–350 fF/s; Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1), therefore slow endocytosis unlikely contributes to the millisecond-order site-clearance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Slow endocytosis unlikely contributes to the millisecond-order site-clearance.
source: However, the rate of slow endocytosis (29 fF/s) is ~10 times slower than fast endocytosis (250–350 fF/s; Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1), therefore slow endocytosis unlikely contributes to the millisecond-order site-clearance.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data on endocytosis rates.

claim: Slow endocytosis may play a house-keeping role in release site-clearance.
source: However, without slow endocytosis, the vesicular membrane remaining after spontaneous exocytosis would accumulate and congest release sites. Thus, slow endocytosis may play a house-keeping role in release site-clearance.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the role of slow endocytosis.

claim: At the calyx of Held, scaffold protein inhibitors significantly enhanced the early phase of synaptic depression (starting at the 2nd stimulation at 100 Hz) like endocytic blockers.
source: At the calyx of Held, scaffold protein inhibitors significantly enhanced the early phase of synaptic depression (starting at the 2nd stimulation at 100 Hz; Figure 4B1) like endocytic blockers (Figure 2B1; Figure 5A and B), despite that they do not block endocytosis (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B1, 3, 4B1, and 5A-B.

claim: Scaffold protein inhibitors do not block endocytosis at the calyx of Held.
source: At the calyx of Held, scaffold protein inhibitors significantly enhanced the early phase of synaptic depression (starting at the 2nd stimulation at 100 Hz; Figure 4B1) like endocytic blockers (Figure 2B1; Figure 5A and B), despite that they do not block endocytosis (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The actin-dependent scaffold-machinery operates for rapid vesicular replenishment predominantly at fast synapses, whereas it is non-functional at relatively slow synapses.
source: Therefore, it is likely that the actin-dependent scaffold-machinery operates for rapid vesicular replenishment predominantly at fast synapses, whereas it is non-functional at relatively slow synapses.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing differential effects at fast versus slow synapses.

claim: The endocytosis-dependent site-clearance mechanism seems to be a universal phenomenon supporting vesicular replenishment among fast and slow mammalian central synapses.
source: In contrast, the endocytosis-dependent site-clearance mechanism seems to be a universal phenomenon supporting vesicular replenishment among fast and slow mammalian central synapses.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing endocytic effects at both types of synapses.

claim: Latrunculin-B reportedly inhibits vesicular docking by limiting replacement pool filling during high-frequency inputs at parallel fiber (PF)-molecular layer interneuron synapses in cerebellar slices.
source: Latrunculin-B reportedly inhibits vesicular docking by limiting replacement pool filling during high-frequency inputs at parallel fiber (PF)-molecular layer interneuron synapses in cerebellar slices (Miki et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Miki et al., 2016.

claim: The PF-molecular layer interneuron synapse is adapted to respond to high-frequency inputs, like other cerebellar synapses.
source: This synapse is adapted to respond to high-frequency inputs, like other cerebellar synapses (e.g. Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014.

claim: Latrunculin A and Latrunculin B are equipotent for STD enhancement at the calyx of Held in 1.3 mM [Ca2+] at PT.
source: Thus, Latrunculin A (20 μM) and Latrunculin B (15 μM) are equipotent for STD enhancement in these experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Control STD level in 1.3 mM [Ca2+] (~0.4) was significantly less than 2.0 mM [Ca2+] (~0.3; p=0.002, t-test).
source: When the data are compared between 1.3 mM [Ca2+] and 2.0 mM [Ca2+], STD levels after Latrunculin A perfusion are not different (p>0.05, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), whereas control STD level in 1.3 mM [Ca2+] (~0.4) was significantly less than 2.0 mM [Ca2+] (~0.3; p=0.002, t-test; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Physiological 1.3 mM [Ca2+] revealed a robust STD-counteracting function of F-actin.
source: Thus, physiological 1.3 mM [Ca2+] revealed a robust STD-counteracting function of F-actin.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data comparing different calcium concentrations.

claim: Ca2+-dependent recovery (CDR) component of tens of milliseconds time constant is produced by strong stimulation at the calyx of Held at RT.
source: Regarding the recovery from STD, Ca2+-dependent recovery (CDR) component of tens of milliseconds time constant is produced by strong stimulation at the calyx of Held at RT (Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998) and inhibited by Latrunculin B (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998 and Lee et al., 2013.

claim: CDR is inhibited by Latrunculin B.
source: Regarding the recovery from STD, Ca2+-dependent recovery (CDR) component of tens of milliseconds time constant is produced by strong stimulation at the calyx of Held at RT (Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998) and inhibited by Latrunculin B (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2013.

claim: CDR is also observed after STD induced by 100 Hz stimulation at PT and blocked by Latrunculin A pretreatment (20 μM) in 2.0 mM [Ca2+].
source: CDR is also observed after STD induced by 100 Hz stimulation at PT and blocked by Latrunculin A pretreatment (20 μM) in 2.0 mM [Ca2+] (Piriya Ananda Babu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Piriya Ananda Babu et al., 2020.

claim: Latrunculin-sensitive fast recovery component was absent in 1.3 mM [Ca2+].
source: However, such Latrunculin-sensitive fast recovery component was absent in 1.3 mM [Ca2+] (Figure 4B2, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: CDR may operate only when excessive Ca2+ enters during massive presynaptic activation.
source: Thus, CDR may operate only when excessive Ca2+ enters during massive presynaptic activation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental data.

claim: At hippocampal excitatory synapses, short-term increase in glutamate release induces long-term potentiation (LTP) of excitatory transmission.
source: At hippocampal excitatory synapses, short-term increase in glutamate release induces long-term potentiation (LTP) of excitatory transmission.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about hippocampal synaptic plasticity.

claim: From physiological viewpoints, endocytosis-dependent site clearance may play a critical role in the induction of LTP underlying memory formation.
source: Thus, from physiological viewpoints, endocytosis-dependent site clearance may play a critical role in the induction of LTP underlying memory formation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Latrunculin-A blocks ultra-fast endocytosis (UFE) in hippocampal culture.
source: This was somewhat unexpected since in hippocampal culture Latrunculin-A blocks ultra-fast endocytosis (UFE, Watanabe et al., 2013), which occurs preferentially at physiological temperature (Watanabe et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Watanabe et al., 2013 and 2014.

claim: UFE occurs preferentially at physiological temperature.
source: This was somewhat unexpected since in hippocampal culture Latrunculin-A blocks ultra-fast endocytosis (UFE, Watanabe et al., 2013), which occurs preferentially at physiological temperature (Watanabe et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Watanabe et al., 2014.

claim: The physiological role of UFE in hippocampal synaptic transmission remains unclear.
source: Since Latrunculin A and B are equipotent in enhancing STD at calyceal synapses in 1.3 mM [Ca 2+] aCSF at PT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D), the physiological role of UFE in hippocampal synaptic transmission remains unclear.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing lack of effect at hippocampal synapses.

claim: Experiments were performed in accordance with the guidelines of the Physiological Society of Japan and animal experiment regulations at Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology Graduate University.
source: All experiments were performed in accordance with the guidelines of the Physiological Society of Japan and animal experiment regulations at Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology Graduate University.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental procedures and ethical compliance.

claim: C57BL/6J mice of either sex after hearing onset (postnatal day 13–15) were used for the experiment.
source: C57BL/6J mice of either sex after hearing onset (postnatal day 13–15) were used for the experiment and animals were maintained on a 12 hr light/dark cycle with food and water ad libitum.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects and conditions.

claim: Transverse slices (200 μm thick) containing the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (MNTB) or parasagittal slices (300 μm) containing the hippocampus were cut using a vibratome.
source: Following decapitation of C57BL/6J mice under isoflurane anesthesia, brains were isolated and transverse slices (200 μm thick) containing the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (MNTB) or parasagittal slices (300 μm) containing the hippocampus were cut using a vibratome (VT1200S, Leica) in ice-cold artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF, see below) with reduced Ca2+ (0.1 mM) and increased Mg2+ (2.9 mM) concentrations and with NaCl replaced by 200 mM sucrose.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Slices were incubated for 1 hr at 37°C in standard aCSF.
source: Slices were incubated for 1 hr at 37°C in standard aCSF containing (in mM); 115 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 25 NaHCO3, 1.25 NaH2PO4, 1.3 or 2.0 CaCl2, 1 MgCl2, 10 glucose, 3 myo-inositol, 2 sodium pyruvate, and 0.4 sodium ascorbate (pH 7.3–7.4 when bubbled with 95% O2 and 5% CO2, 285–290 mOsm).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.
